name: cbp-cld
description: Model version c4beec2, the first seven characters of the SHA-256 of cld.json. A copy for milestones: the current model is the page https://jordyzuidam2003-bot.github.io/zeeland-cld/, built from https://github.com/jordyzuidam2003-bot/zeeland-cld.

attributes.name: Actor
values: Banks lending to the island's farmers
Buyers and processors of the island's crops

attributes.label: Hotter, drier summers
attributes.description: Meteorological drought (KNMI'23): higher evaporation, summer precipitation deficit, and lower river discharge.

attributes.label: Sea-level rise
attributes.description: Rising sea level (KNMI'23 scenarios); increases hydrostatic pressure of marine water on polders and estuaries.

attributes.label: Wetter winters
attributes.description: Increased winter precipitation, providing potential recharge volume if retained.

attributes.label: Crop water demand
attributes.description: The water the crops use in the growing season when they have enough, whatever its origin: the crop's evapotranspiration, set by the weather (radiation, air temperature, humidity and wind speed) and by the crop and its stage of growth (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56, a guide to crop water use that holds wherever the crop grows). It follows the weather within the season, highest in sunny, warm and dry weather: an Auxiliary.
attributes.sources: Allen, R. G., Pereira, L. S., Raes, D., & Smith, M. (1998). Crop evapotranspiration: Guidelines for computing crop water requirements (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56). FAO. https://www.fao.org/4/x0490e/x0490e00.htm

attributes.label: Estuary salt intrusion
attributes.description: Marine water penetrating further inland into estuaries and surface canals when sea levels rise and river discharge drops.

attributes.label: Freshwater lens  recharge
attributes.description: The rain that soaks in and refills the rainwater lens: mostly the winter's rain surplus, since in summer most of the rain evaporates (van Beekom et al., 1953a, for the Netherlands). On Schouwen-Duiveland it soaks deep into the dunes and the sandy creek ridges, while in the low polders upward saline seepage keeps it within the clay top layer and tile drains carry much of it off during each rain; recharge, seepage and drainage depth together set the lens's thickness (de Louw et al., 2011, measured on the island).
attributes.sources:
van Beekom, C. W. C., van den Berg, C., de Boer, Th. A., van der Molen, W. H., Verhoeven, B., Westerhof, J. J., & Zuur, A. J. (1953a). Reclaiming land flooded with salt water: I. Salt. Netherlands Journal of Agricultural Science, 1(3), 153–163. https://library.wur.nl/ojs/index.php/njas/article/view/17866
de Louw, P. G. B., Eeman, S., Siemon, B., Voortman, B. R., Gunnink, J., van Baaren, E. S., & Oude Essink, G. H. P. (2011). Shallow rainwater lenses in deltaic areas with saline seepage. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 15(12), 3659–3678. https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-15-3659-2011

attributes.label: Freshwater lens  thickness
attributes.description: The thickness of the fresh rainwater lens on top of the saline groundwater, from the surface to the middle of the mixing zone between them. On Schouwen-Duiveland it is about 2 m on average in the low-lying polders with saline seepage, under 2 m over more than half of the 56 km² surveyed, and 5 to 15 m under the sandy creek ridges (de Louw et al., 2011, measured on the island from a helicopter and on the ground); lenses reach about 30 m under the creek ridges and the dunes, and nearly 100 m under the dunes (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). A Stock: a year's recharge barely moves it (Freshwater lens recharge → Freshwater lens thickness).
attributes.sources:
de Louw, P. G. B., Eeman, S., Siemon, B., Voortman, B. R., Gunnink, J., van Baaren, E. S., & Oude Essink, G. H. P. (2011). Shallow rainwater lenses in deltaic areas with saline seepage. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 15(12), 3659–3678. https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-15-3659-2011
Kaandorp, V. P., Davids, T., de Louw, P. G. B., Roelandse, A., Noordegraaf, I., Krajenbrink, H. J., Schout, G., Raat, K. J., & van Veelen, P. C. (2022). Samenwerken voor zoet water Schouwen-Duiveland – van pilots naar grootschalige toepassing: Eindrapport (11205909-000-BGS-0003). Deltares, for Gemeente Schouwen-Duiveland. https://livinglabschouwen-duiveland.nl/sites/default/files/2022-07/112059~1.PDF

attributes.label: Land subsidence
attributes.description: Peat oxidation and clay consolidation caused by low drainage levels, lowering the land surface relative to sea level.

attributes.label: Polder surface  elevation (NAP)
attributes.description: Physical land surface elevation of the polder (-1.5m to -3.5m NAP), lowered by subsidence. Tidal silt, let in through a wisselpolder, would barely raise it on this island: the Grevelingen has no tide, and the Oosterschelde has too little silt to raise polders on a large scale (De Mesel et al., 2013). Since the storm surge barrier its channels carry 52–70% less suspended sediment (Ma et al., 2014), under 10 mg/l near Zierikzee, and its salt marshes rise 3–10 mm a year (van Maldegem & de Jong, 2004), against 16–32 mm on young marshes along the Westerschelde (De Mesel et al., 2013).
attributes.sources:
De Mesel, I., Ysebaert, T., & Kamermans, P. (2013). Klimaatbestendige dijken: Het concept wisselpolders (Rapport C072/13). IMARES Wageningen UR. https://www.vliz.be/imisdocs/publications/289823.pdf
Ma, Z., Ysebaert, T., van der Wal, D., de Jong, D. J., Li, X., & Herman, P. M. J. (2014). Long-term salt marsh vertical accretion in a tidal bay with reduced sediment supply. Estuarine, Coastal and Shelf Science, 146, 14–23. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecss.2014.05.001
van Maldegem, D., & de Jong, D. (2004). Opwassen of verdrinken: Sedimentaanvoer naar schorren in de Oosterschelde, een zandhongerig gedempt getijdesysteem (Werkdocument RIKZ/AB/2003/826x). Rijkswaterstaat, Rijksinstituut voor Kust en Zee. https://edepot.wur.nl/174582

attributes.label: Root zone salinity
attributes.description: The salt concentration of the soil water in the crop root zone. Salt harms a crop in two phases: at once osmotically, slowing the growth of young leaves, and more slowly as sodium (Na+) or chloride (Cl-) builds up in the leaves, ageing the older ones early (Munns & Tester, 2008, a review of plant physiology, which holds wherever the crop grows). It rises in a dry summer as the soil dries out and salt rises by capillary rise, and falls with the winter's rain surplus, which washes the topsoil of well-drained soil free of salt in one winter and that of badly drained soil in two or three (van Beekom et al., 1953a, measured after the floods in Zeeland): within the year where the soil drains well, so an Auxiliary.
attributes.sources:
Munns, R., & Tester, M. (2008). Mechanisms of salinity tolerance. Annual Review of Plant Biology, 59, 651–681. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.arplant.59.032607.092911
van Beekom, C. W. C., van den Berg, C., de Boer, Th. A., van der Molen, W. H., Verhoeven, B., Westerhof, J. J., & Zuur, A. J. (1953a). Reclaiming land flooded with salt water: I. Salt. Netherlands Journal of Agricultural Science, 1(3), 153–163. https://library.wur.nl/ojs/index.php/njas/article/view/17866

attributes.label: Saline seepage (kwel)
attributes.description: Upward hydrostatic pressure pushing salty groundwater through clay/peat layers (diffuse or via boils).

attributes.label: Soil structure
attributes.description: The soil's aggregates and pores, which set how fast water soaks in: well-drained clay with its structure intact let the winter's rain surplus soak through almost completely, while clay whose structure sodium had broken down became impervious and sticky when wet (van Beekom et al., 1953a, 1953b, measured after the floods in Zeeland). A Stock: once broken down, it recovers over years (Root zone salinity → Soil structure). Workability, which structure and wetness both shape, is Spring workability of the fields.
attributes.sources:
van Beekom, C. W. C., van den Berg, C., de Boer, Th. A., van der Molen, W. H., Verhoeven, B., Westerhof, J. J., & Zuur, A. J. (1953a). Reclaiming land flooded with salt water: I. Salt. Netherlands Journal of Agricultural Science, 1(3), 153–163. https://library.wur.nl/ojs/index.php/njas/article/view/17866
van Beekom, C. W. C., van den Berg, C., de Boer, Th. A., van der Molen, W. H., Verhoeven, B., Westerhof, J. J., & Zuur, A. J. (1953b). Reclaiming land flooded with salt water: II. Exchangeable cations. Netherlands Journal of Agricultural Science, 1(4), 224–244. https://library.wur.nl/ojs/index.php/njas/article/view/17860

attributes.label: Upconing of salt  groundwater
attributes.description: Upward cone of the salt-freshwater interface beneath pumping irrigation wells as the freshwater lens thins.

attributes.label: Brackish irrigation  water use
attributes.description: Irrigation with salinised surface or well water, when fresh water falls short.

attributes.label: Farmers' demand for  deep polder drainage
attributes.description: Farmers' wish for low ditch levels in spring, so heavy machinery can work the fields early, which they put to the water board as it makes its water level plans.

attributes.label: Fresh water supplied  to the island
attributes.description: Fresh water brought to the island's farms from outside it in the growing season (present in Tholen and Zeeuws-Vlaanderen; absent on Walcheren, the Bevelanden and Schouwen-Duiveland). It needs a supply route, and in drought it is what the national distribution leaves for the route to carry.

attributes.label: Freshwater  availability for crops
attributes.description: Fresh water crops can draw on in the growing season: soil moisture over the lens, and what farmers pump or have supplied.

attributes.label: Freshwater storage  measures
attributes.description: On-farm and sub-surface water retention: Freshmaker, ASR-Coastal, creek-ridge infiltration, and adjustable/smart drainage. Whether a farm decides a measure alone or with the water board is a question for a source. Whether a farm wants to store weighs storing against its other ways through a dry summer (pumping, brackish water, other crops), where capacity to invest is whether it can. Stored water pays back over years, which suits a farm that owns its land more than one on a short lease; and where stored water spreads under the neighbours, one farm pays and others gain. Whether either holds a farm back is a question for the group model building session.

attributes.label: Groundwater extraction  for irrigation
attributes.description: Fresh water farmers pump from the fresh groundwater through their own wells, to irrigate or to flush their fields in summer; the water board's pumping stations belong to drainage. The water board sets the rules: a horizontal well at most 6 m below the surface and 80 to 200 m long, at least 200 m from the next well and 50 m from a neighbour's field, pumping at most 800 m³ per hectare and 8,000 m³ per well a year (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026); in Zeeland only from fresh groundwater more than 15 m thick, outside vulnerable areas (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 26). Whose lens a well draws on, the farm's own or one it shares with its neighbours, so that a farm pumping less leaves water to them, is a hypothesis for the group model building session; the rules are written so that a well's effects stay within the farm's own field (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021), an aim of the rules rather than a measurement. Pumping follows the season's shortfall within the year: an Auxiliary.
attributes.sources:
Waterschap Scheldestromen. (2026, May 29). Besluit wijziging artikel 2.9 van de Waterschapsverordening waterschap Scheldestromen (Waterschapsblad 2026, nr. 13978). https://zoek.officielebekendmakingen.nl/wsb-2026-13978.html
Kaandorp, V. P., Davids, T., de Louw, P. G. B., Roelandse, A., Noordegraaf, I., Krajenbrink, H. J., Schout, G., Raat, K. J., & van Veelen, P. C. (2022). Samenwerken voor zoet water Schouwen-Duiveland – van pilots naar grootschalige toepassing: Eindrapport (11205909-000-BGS-0003). Deltares, for Gemeente Schouwen-Duiveland. https://livinglabschouwen-duiveland.nl/sites/default/files/2022-07/112059~1.PDF
Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland. (2021, June 9). Antwoorden op vragen van de statenleden Heerschop en Van der Vliet (PvdA) inzake onttrekkingen grondwater (zaaknummer 54188, aanhangsel tot de notulen van Provinciale Staten nr. 191). https://www.zeeland.nl/sites/default/files/digitaalarchief/IB21_ae4d5ac6.pdf

attributes.label: Objections to land-use  plans
attributes.description: Objections, appeals at the Council of State (Raad van State) and political pressure against plans for the island's water and land, the water board's water level plans among them, which slow, change or stop a plan.

attributes.label: Winter rain drained  away
attributes.description: Winter precipitation rapidly discharged to sea via field drains and pumping stations instead of recharging the lens.

attributes.label: Crop yield
attributes.description: Physical yield per hectare of conventional crops (potatoes, onions, sugar beet) under the prevailing freshwater, soil and workability conditions; what salt takes from their harvest is Harvest lost to salt.

attributes.label: Market demand for  alternative crops
attributes.description: Consumer demand and offtake contracts for novel salt-tolerant or alternative crops (e.g. protein crops).

attributes.label: Local processing  capacity for new crops
attributes.description: Plants and supply chains on or near the island that store, process or sell new salt-tolerant crops. Breeding of tolerant varieties is Salt-tolerant varieties on offer. Buyers and processors build or keep it where they find it worthwhile against processing the crops elsewhere.
attributes.actor: Buyers and processors of the island's crops

attributes.label: Adoption of new  salt-tolerant crops
attributes.description: Hectares under crops new to the island's rotations that tolerate salt (quinoa, samphire, sea aster, field beans), which need other machines, knowledge and buyers than the current crops. Farmers grow one where they find it worthwhile against their current crops; capacity to invest is whether they can, and dependence on the current crops what holds them.

attributes.label: Agricultural land  value
attributes.description: The price farmland sells for (€/ha), set by what buyers expect it to earn; banks value it as collateral in their own risk assessment.

attributes.label: Risk premium on farm  loans
attributes.description: The interest banks charge arable farms above their own funding cost, for the risk they see in the loan.
attributes.actor: Banks lending to the island's farmers

attributes.label: Basel IV capital  requirements
attributes.description: European banking regulations requiring stricter risk weighting on loans when climate/soil risks reduce collateral value.

attributes.label: Dependence on  high-margin  salt-sensitive crops
attributes.description: The share of high-value, salt-sensitive cash crops (seed potatoes, onions) in the rotation, which a farm with high debt payments needs to keep up its income, and which the machines and know-how it would lose by switching tie it to.

attributes.label: Farm income
attributes.description: Farms' revenue from crop sales, set by yield and prices, minus their costs (the water board's levy, interest, their own pumping), per hectare in a year.

attributes.label: Farmers' capacity to  invest
attributes.description: What a farm has left to invest after its debt payments and rent, beside the credit a bank will give it.

attributes.label: Owners' concern about  their land's value
attributes.description: Landowning farmers' concern that their land loses value, from a fall that has happened or from a plan that would lower it. A tenant's concern, losing the lease, is not part of it.

attributes.label: Financial leverage
attributes.description: The farm's debt relative to the value of its assets, the inverse of its solvency (equity as a share of total capital). Land is 70% of an arable farm's balance sheet, so the ratio moves with the land price: arable farms' solvency was 81% in 2018 because their land had risen in value, while their long-term debt had tripled since 2001 to 770,000 euro per farm (van der Meulen et al., 2020).
attributes.sources: van der Meulen, H., van der Meer, R., & van Asseldonk, M. (2020). Financiering transitie naar duurzame landbouw: Inzicht in het huidige financieringslandschap en ontwikkelingen (Rapport 2020-097). Wageningen Economic Research. https://edepot.wur.nl/532092

attributes.label: Arable land in the  polders
attributes.description: Hectares of the island's land farmed as arable land, with conventional or salt-tolerant crops, whoever owns it. It falls when land that changes hands goes to a holder who does not farm it as arable land; what the land becomes then (nature, grassland, water storage) waits for the group's system boundary.

attributes.label: Crop water shortfall
attributes.description: What crops need in the growing season beyond the water they get, fresh or brackish: the gap farmers' water decisions respond to. The island's farms depend wholly on rain and on the fresh groundwater under the dunes, the creek ridges and the thin rainwater lenses of the low polders; with no link to the main freshwater system, no fresh water can be brought in and no ditches flushed in dry periods, so the farms run short of water, as the dry years 2018, 2019 and 2020 showed (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8). It follows the weather within the season: an Auxiliary.
attributes.sources: Kaandorp, V. P., Davids, T., de Louw, P. G. B., Roelandse, A., Noordegraaf, I., Krajenbrink, H. J., Schout, G., Raat, K. J., & van Veelen, P. C. (2022). Samenwerken voor zoet water Schouwen-Duiveland – van pilots naar grootschalige toepassing: Eindrapport (11205909-000-BGS-0003). Deltares, for Gemeente Schouwen-Duiveland. https://livinglabschouwen-duiveland.nl/sites/default/files/2022-07/112059~1.PDF

attributes.label: Flushing salt from the  root zone
attributes.description: Fresh water farmers put on a field to wash salt below the roots, pumped from the lens.

attributes.label: Freshwater supply  route to the island
attributes.description: Pipes or channels that could bring fresh water to the island, as their capacity in a summer; none exists. Who decides on one and who pays is on the facts list under External freshwater supply; news reports say the province has costed a pipeline (unread at the source).

attributes.label: Spring workability of  the fields
attributes.description: Whether heavy machinery can work the fields early in spring without damaging the soil, set by soil structure and by how wet the soil is.

attributes.label: Polder drainage depth
attributes.description: How far below the surface the water board holds the ditch levels in the island's polders, as its water level plans (peilbesluiten) set them; it changes only when the board carries out a new plan.

attributes.label: Water board's plans to  raise ditch levels
attributes.description: Draft or adopted water level plans in which Waterschap Scheldestromen raises a polder's ditch levels, weighing farmers' demand against seepage, subsidence and its pumping costs. Farmers weigh in on these decisions through the seats on its general board reserved for agricultural landowners (the session's understanding, unsourced: on the facts list under Demand for deep polder drainage).

attributes.label: Water board's pumping  costs
attributes.description: What Waterschap Scheldestromen spends on its pumping stations to hold the polders' ditch levels: more water to pump the deeper it drains, the more seepage and winter rain come in and the lower the land lies.

attributes.label: Water board levy on  farmland
attributes.description: What the water board charges owners and users of farmland for its water management, pumping included.

attributes.label: Harvest lost to salt
attributes.description: The conventional crops' harvest that salt in the root zone takes, over the island's fields still under them.

attributes.label: Margin given up on  high-margin crops
attributes.description: The margin a farm forgoes on fields it moves from its high-margin current crops to salt-tolerant ones, largest on fresh land, where the current crops still do well.

attributes.label: Farms with a successor
attributes.description: Arable farms on the island whose farmer has someone to take the farm over.

attributes.label: Harvest of new crops  to process
attributes.description: The volume of new salt-tolerant crops within reach of a processing plant on or near the island, from the island's growers and from growers elsewhere.

attributes.label: Net price for new  crops after transport
attributes.description: What farmers on the island get for new salt-tolerant crops once transport to the processor is paid, set by processors on and off the island.

attributes.label: Growers of new crops  elsewhere
attributes.description: Farmers off the island growing the same new crops, whose harvest a local plant could also process.

attributes.label: Processing of new  crops elsewhere
attributes.description: Plants off the island that buy and process new salt-tolerant crops, which set the price the island's growers can get beside a local plant.

attributes.label: Adoption of  salt-tolerant  varieties
attributes.description: Hectares under salt-tolerant varieties of the current crops (potato, onion), which use the same machines, storage and know-how. Farmers grow one where they find it worthwhile against the variety they grow now.

attributes.label: Salt-tolerant  varieties on offer
attributes.description: Salt-tolerant varieties of the current crops that breeders bring to market, and their yield; breeding lies outside the CLD's scale.

attributes.label: Machines and storage  for the current crops
attributes.description: The planters, harvesters and stores farms own for their current crops, built up over years and renewed when worn.

attributes.label: Capital lost on  switching to new crops
attributes.description: The machines, storage and know-how a farm writes off when it moves fields to a new crop that cannot use them; what it keeps using or sells is not lost. Salt-tolerant varieties of the current crops lose little of it.

attributes.label: Farmers' knowledge of  new crops
attributes.description: What the island's farmers know about growing and selling new salt-tolerant crops, from their own fields, their neighbours' and advisers.

attributes.label: Spending on keeping  the current crops
attributes.description: What farms invest in carrying on with their current crops: wells and irrigation, drains, new machines and storage.

attributes.label: Banks' risk assessment  of farm loans
attributes.description: The risk a bank sees in lending to an arable farm: its solvency, its collateral at the bank's own valuation, and plans that may change what the land can earn.

attributes.label: Bank credit to farms
attributes.description: New loans and refinancing that banks grant the island's arable farms.
attributes.actor: Banks lending to the island's farmers

attributes.label: Debt payments
attributes.description: Interest and repayments farms owe on their loans in a year.

attributes.label: World prices of  conventional crops
attributes.description: The prices of potatoes, onions and sugar beet on the markets the island's crops are sold on, which its farms cannot move: what carrying on is weighed against.

attributes.label: Farmers' trust in  government
attributes.description: How far the island's farmers expect public bodies to keep their commitments on water and land (compensation, their say over their land).

attributes.label: Expropriation of  farmland
attributes.description: Farmland a public body takes for a public purpose, with compensation, after a legal procedure; which body can do so on the island is on the facts list under Concern about expropriation and devaluation.

attributes.label: Farmers' wish to keep  their land
attributes.description: How strongly farmers hold on to their land beyond its money value: family land, growing up on it. Whether anything on the map moves it, at succession perhaps, is a question for the group model building session.

attributes.label: Farmland changing  hands
attributes.description: Hectares of the island's farmland sold, expropriated or passed on to a new holder in a year: at a forced sale, a retirement without a successor, or otherwise.

attributes.label: Farmland planned for  other uses
attributes.description: Hectares of the island's farmland that Gemeente Schouwen-Duiveland's land-use plan (its omgevingsplan, with the changes it drafts to it) designates for a use other than arable farming, such as nature, water storage, housing or recreation. Which plans the municipality makes for the island's farmland, and where objections enter them, is on the facts list under Objections to land-use plans.
Higher temperatures increase evapotranspiration and crop water requirements.
Low summer river discharge allows seawater to penetrate further inland.
Summer precipitation deficit and high evaporation reduce natural recharge.
Rising sea level pushes marine water further into estuaries.
Higher sea level increases hydrostatic pressure beneath dikes.
More winter precipitation increases potential infiltration into the soil.
Higher winter rainfall peaks are mostly discharged under conventional drainage.
Salinisation of surface canals makes intake water for irrigation brackish.

Rainwater infiltration builds up the floating freshwater lens, but slowly: the lens is a stock that a year's recharge barely moves. In the thin polder lenses of Schouwen-Duiveland the mixing zone shifts at most 0.1 m within a year, with vertical flow of at most 1.2 mm per day (de Louw et al., 2011). Under a creek ridge, raising the winter water table 0.5 m thickened a 13–15 m lens by 6–8 m in ten years, and the lens had not reached its new thickness yet (Pauw et al., 2015, a model result for a creek ridge on Walcheren, which transfers since the island's sandy creek ridges also take in rain over saline groundwater: de Louw et al., 2011). So a change in recharge takes years to a decade to show in the lens.
attributes.sources:
de Louw, P. G. B., Eeman, S., Siemon, B., Voortman, B. R., Gunnink, J., van Baaren, E. S., & Oude Essink, G. H. P. (2011). Shallow rainwater lenses in deltaic areas with saline seepage. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 15(12), 3659–3678. https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-15-3659-2011
Pauw, P. S., van Baaren, E. S., Visser, M., de Louw, P. G. B., & Oude Essink, G. H. P. (2015). Increasing a freshwater lens below a creek ridge using a controlled artificial recharge and drainage system: A case study in the Netherlands. Hydrogeology Journal, 23(7), 1415–1430. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10040-015-1264-z

attributes.description: Where the lens is thin, saline groundwater lies just below the roots and reaches the root zone by capillary rise. In the island's low polders with saline seepage the lens is about 2 m thick, its mixing zone in the clay top layer, and capillary rise of saline groundwater is very likely now, possibly damaging crops (de Louw et al., 2011, measured on Schouwen-Duiveland); the topsoil there is fresh thanks to the rainwater lens, which makes farming possible, and these low polders of heavy clay make up a large part of the island (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 4, 10). Under the creek ridges and the dunes the lens is 5 m thick or more (Freshwater lens thickness), so the link holds in the low polders. Within the year: in a dry season, with the groundwater below the drains, the flow there is only upward (de Louw et al., 2011).
attributes.sources:
de Louw, P. G. B., Eeman, S., Siemon, B., Voortman, B. R., Gunnink, J., van Baaren, E. S., & Oude Essink, G. H. P. (2011). Shallow rainwater lenses in deltaic areas with saline seepage. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 15(12), 3659–3678. https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-15-3659-2011
Kaandorp, V. P., Davids, T., de Louw, P. G. B., Roelandse, A., Noordegraaf, I., Krajenbrink, H. J., Schout, G., Raat, K. J., & van Veelen, P. C. (2022). Samenwerken voor zoet water Schouwen-Duiveland – van pilots naar grootschalige toepassing: Eindrapport (11205909-000-BGS-0003). Deltares, for Gemeente Schouwen-Duiveland. https://livinglabschouwen-duiveland.nl/sites/default/files/2022-07/112059~1.PDF

attributes.description: A thicker freshwater lens buffers against salt upconing under wells.
A thicker lens provides a larger buffer of fresh soil moisture in summer.

Peat oxidation and clay settling lower the land surface relative to NAP at millimetres a year, so a decimetre takes decades: Dutch land below sea level is still subsiding up to 1 m per century, fastest in peat areas (Oude Essink et al., 2010). A rate for Schouwen-Duiveland's clay polders is not yet sourced.
attributes.sources: Oude Essink, G. H. P., van Baaren, E. S., & de Louw, P. G. B. (2010). Effects of climate change on coastal groundwater systems: A modeling study in the Netherlands. Water Resources Research, 46, W00F04. https://doi.org/10.1029/2009WR008719

attributes.description: Higher polder elevation reduces the hydraulic head difference driving upward saline seepage.

Salt in the root zone puts sodium (Na+) on the clay in place of calcium (Ca2+); once fresh water washes the salt out, clay that holds much sodium disperses: its aggregates and pores collapse, with troubles to be expected above 1 m.e. of exchangeable sodium per 100 g of dry soil. The delay is on the way back: structure collapses within the first winter after the salt leaches out, but the clay only recovers as calcium replaces the sodium again, about 0.7 m.e. Na per 100 g a year, which takes 5 to 10 years on heavy clay and about a year on light soil (van Beekom et al., 1953b, after the 1945 and 1953 floods in Zeeland). Seawater flooding is a much larger salt dose than seepage; soils that took up less sodium recover faster, and no source read shows how much sodium the island's seepage puts on its clay.

Exchangeable cations. Netherlands Journal of Agricultural Science, 1(4), 224–244. https://library.wur.nl/ojs/index.php/njas/article/view/17860

attributes.description: Upward saline groundwater erodes and thins the floating freshwater lens from below.
Capillary rise brings saline seepage water into the root zone.

Rain recharges the lens only once it has soaked into the soil. Before the floods, Zeeland's well-drained clay let the winter's rain surplus soak through almost completely; once sodium had broken down the structure of the topsoil, it became impervious and sticky when wet, part of the rain ran off over the surface and pools stood on the land, the more so the heavier the clay (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 157; 1953b, p. 233, measured in the flooded polders of Zeeland, by R1's own mechanism). Within the year: the structure a soil has in a winter sets how much of that winter's rain soaks in. Whether what soaks in reaches the lens or leaves through the drains is set by the drainage depth and the seepage (de Louw et al., 2011).

attributes.description: Good soil structure lets roots grow and crops emerge.
Structural soil health and low salinity determine the intrinsic value of arable land.
Salt water drawn upward contaminates the upper soil and irrigation wells.
Evaporation of brackish irrigation water leaves salt behind in the topsoil.
Fresh water supplied from outside adds to what crops can draw on.
Active infiltration (creek-ridge infiltration, Freshmaker, ASR-Coastal) builds up the freshwater lens; retained drain water reaches it through Winter rain drained away.
Adjustable drains and storage keep winter water in the polder instead of discharging it.

What farmers pump beyond what the rain puts back thins the lens, the boundary with the saline groundwater below rising: the water board's limit of 800 m³ per hectare a year rests on the balance between recharge by rain, irrigation water and extraction, set to keep the fresh groundwater in stock and the fresh-salt boundary from rising (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026), and pumping too fast risks salinisation (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 20–21). Within those rules the effects are meant to stay within the farm's field, with in principle no depletion, and Deltares's modelling of the rules (2018) found them generally enough to prevent strong salinisation under and around the well (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021, for Zeeland). How fast the lens responds to pumping, no source read shows.

attributes.description: Pumping groundwater draws the underlying salt-fresh interface upward into a cone.
Water evacuated via drains cannot infiltrate to refill the freshwater lens.
Higher physical yield increases sales revenue per hectare.

New salt-tolerant crops need less water than the current crops: no source read shows it. FAO-56 gives field beans the same peak water use as potatoes and wheat (a mid-season crop coefficient of 1.15, against 1.20 for sugar beet and 1.05 for onions), over a shorter season in Europe, about 90 days sown in May against 145 for potatoes planted in April (Allen et al., 1998, Tables 11 and 12, values for a sub-humid climate and a general guide); it lists neither quinoa, samphire nor sea aster, and no source read shows whether the halophytes need less water or take salt water instead.

A fall in the land's value that has happened, through salt in R6: does a farm whose land lost value object harder to the next plan? Through its solvency, yes (−); where compensation pays more than the land would fetch on the market, the concern may fall instead (+). A hypothesis for the group model building session, with both signs as the question to farmers.

With the same mortgage, a lower land value is a higher debt relative to the farm's assets: land is 70% of an arable farm's balance sheet, and its rise in value is what made arable farms' solvency 81% in 2018 (van der Meulen et al., 2020). A high solvency makes new credit easier and cheaper to get; the debt itself does not shrink when the land loses value.

attributes.description: Stricter European banking rules require more capital against climate-exposed loans, which banks price in.
Potatoes and onions require dry, warm soils in early spring to bear heavy machinery.
High-value salt-sensitive crops require intensive freshwater irrigation during dry spells.
A farm that relies on high margins can give fewer hectares to lower-margin new crops.
Sustained productivity and profitability underpin high market prices for farmland.
Higher farm income generates internal cash flow for adaptive investments.
Capacity to invest decides whether a farm can pay for a storage measure, not whether it wants to.
Capacity to invest decides whether a farm can pay for the switch (new machines, the first years of a new crop), not whether it wants to.
Concern about uncompensated loss leads farmers and their organisations to object, appeal and lobby against such plans.

Once a crop has drawn the root zone down beyond the water it can take up easily, it uses less water than it needs, in proportion to what is left in the root zone (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8): the shortfall is the part of the demand that rain, soil moisture and irrigation leave unmet, so the more the crops need, the larger it is. On Schouwen-Duiveland's clay a crop that has come up well gets through the summer on the soil's good supply of moisture, so the shortfall falls mostly at germination early in the season, when a small gift of about 20 mm would cover it; onions also need water while they grow (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 27, 31, 38, from talks with the island's farmers). Within the year.

attributes.description: The more fresh water crops can draw on, the smaller the shortfall.

Farmers pump more fresh groundwater as the shortfall grows: the water board registered a considerable increase in extractions in recent years, which the more extreme drought certainly influenced, so the volume pumped rises in dry years (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021, for Zeeland, whose farms pump under the same rules as the island's). On Schouwen-Duiveland the farms get their fresh water from rain and from the fresh groundwater; the shallow groundwater and the ditches are brackish to salt, and no water can be brought in (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8). They may pump only from fresh groundwater more than 15 m thick, under the creek ridges and the dunes (p. 26): in the low polders the farmers talked to do not irrigate, while on the creek ridges a few pump from deep drains, an arable farmer about 20 mm at germination and a livestock farmer for grassland through the summer (pp. 27–28, 43). So the link runs where a farm has fresh groundwater under it. Within the year.

attributes.description: What farmers pump is fresh water their crops get: what pumping gains them.
When fresh water falls short, farmers irrigate with brackish ditch or well water.
Brackish water still waters the crop, so the shortfall shrinks while salt builds up.
Crops that get too little water yield less; not irrigating means taking that loss.
The saltier the root zone, the more fresh water farmers use to wash the salt down.
Fresh water washes salt below the roots, for now.
The water for flushing is pumped from the lens.
A farm pays for its own pumping, part of its costs.
A supply route carries fresh water to the island.

Dry summers lower river discharge, so less river water is left to supply: a route can only carry what summer discharge and the national distribution in drought (the verdringingsreeks, IenW and Rijkswaterstaat) leave for the region, outside the CLD's scale.
Farmers short of water, through their organisations, ask for a supply route, and the deciding body weighs it.
A soil with good structure carries machinery sooner after rain.
Deeper ditch levels dry the topsoil sooner in spring.
Fields that can be worked in time are planted and harvested in time.
Where fields stay too wet to work, farmers ask for lower ditch levels: what deep drainage gains them.
Low water tables expose peat to oxygen and let clay shrink and settle.
Lower ditch levels increase the pressure gradient between deep saline groundwater and the polder.
Deeper drainage carries more winter rain off to the sea.
A plan carried out raises the ditch levels, after its procedure (a draft, objections, the decision, appeals).
The water board weighs farmers' need for low spring levels against raising them.
Seepage and the salt it brings give the water board a reason to raise the levels.
Subsidence gives the water board a reason to raise the levels.
Rising pumping costs give the water board a reason to raise the levels.
Objections delay, change or stop a plan to raise the levels, while it is pending; with none pending, they change nothing.
The deeper the board drains, the more water its pumping stations lift.
Seepage water has to be pumped out too.
Winter rain drained away is pumped out of the polder.
The lower the land lies, the higher the board must lift its water.
The board passes its pumping costs on through its levy.
The levy is part of a farm's costs.
Osmotic stress and chloride toxicity take part of the salt-sensitive crops' harvest.
Harvest lost to salt is income lost.
A field moved to a new salt-tolerant crop no longer loses a conventional harvest to salt.
A salt-tolerant variety loses less of its harvest to salt.
A field moved to a new crop gives up the current crop's margin.
A tolerant variety may yield or sell for less than the variety it replaces, on fresh land most.
Margin given up is income given up.
Higher prices for the current crops raise the income from carrying on.
As harvests get worse, farmers find storing water more worthwhile, and those who can pay for it store more.
Water stored now pays back over years, which suits a farm with a successor.
What a storage measure costs comes out of the money left to invest.
The saltier the field, the more a tolerant variety is worth against the current one, so the more farmers grow it, perhaps only past a threshold.
Better tolerant varieties on the market make switching more worthwhile, so more farmers grow them.
The saltier the field, the more a new salt-tolerant crop is worth against the current crops, so the more farmers grow it, perhaps only past a threshold.
Assured offtake lowers the risk of a new crop, so more farmers grow it.
A better price after transport makes a new crop more worthwhile, so more farmers grow it.
Farmers who know how to grow and sell a new crop find it less risky, so more of them grow it.
Growing a new crop, on their own fields or their neighbours', teaches farmers how.
Switching costs (machines, the first years of a new crop) come out of the money left to invest.
More hectares of new crops on the island, more harvest to process.
Growers elsewhere add to the harvest a local plant could draw on.
More harvest within reach makes a local plant more worthwhile, so processors build or keep capacity on or near the island rather than process the crops elsewhere.
Stable demand makes investing in processing more worthwhile.
A plant nearby cuts transport, so farmers keep more of the price.
Processors elsewhere compete for the harvest and set the price a local plant must match.
A farm that keeps its current crops keeps investing in their machines and storage.
Growing the current crops year after year builds up know-how in growing, storing and selling them, and that know-how is of little use for a new crop.
The more a farm owns for its current crops, the more a switch to a new crop writes off.
What a farm would lose by switching ties it to its current crops.
Money left to invest can go to carrying on: wells, irrigation, drains, a new harvester.
A farm tied to its current crops spends on keeping them.
What it spends there is not left for other uses.
A new harvester or store adds to the capital for the current crops.
Wells and irrigation let a farm pump more.
A farm with less equity against its debt is a riskier loan.
A plan that may change what the land can earn enters a bank's risk analysis before it is decided.
Banks lend less to farms they see as riskier.
Banks charge more for loans they see as riskier.
Credit is part of what a farm can invest.
New loans add to a farm's debt against its assets.
More debt, more to pay each year.
A higher premium raises the interest farms pay.
Interest is part of a farm's costs.
A farm with high debt payments keeps its lucrative but salt-sensitive crops to meet them.
Farms that cannot refinance sell up.
Highly leveraged farms are the ones sold in a forced sale or bankruptcy.
A farm with a successor stays with the family; one without is sold when its farmer retires.
Farmers attached to their land sell it later, often only when forced.
Expropriated land passes to the public body that takes it, after a legal procedure.
Land that changes hands leaves arable farming when its next holder does not farm it.
Where arable farming still pays for a buyer or successor, the next holder keeps the land arable.
The more hectares of arable land in a polder, the more farmers there ask for low spring levels.
A farm that pays finds a successor more easily.
A plan to raise the ditch levels makes owners fear their land will lose value.
Farmers who trust that public bodies keep their commitments object less.
Farmers attached to their land resist plans for it beyond what it is worth in money.
Objections and appeals delay, change or stop plans for the island's water and land after public bodies announced them, and plans changed or dropped teach farmers not to count on the next one.
Where owners will not sell, a public body may expropriate.
Land taken by force lowers farmers' trust in government.
Objections delay, change or stop a plan in which the municipality designates farmland for another use, while it is pending; with none pending, they change nothing.
A plan that designates farmland for another use leads its owners and the farmers who work it to object, appeal and lobby against it.
Farmland the plan designates for another use leaves arable farming once the plan is carried out on it; how long that takes waits for a source.
